column1: # rule|intent|action|question

repetition.expansion|present|Look at the ideas you have started exploring. Mark one that has produced something you can examine and one that still exists only as a possibility.|Where is exploration teaching you something, and where is it only multiplying unfinished starts?

repetition.expansion|crossroads|Choose two possible directions for the piece. Describe the smallest trial of each and compare the time and materials those trials require.|Which direction could you explore without promising a finished project too soon?

repetition.expansion|action|Give one new possibility ten minutes in a rough sketch, phrase or study. Keep the result even if you decide not to continue it.|What did making this small version reveal that imagining it did not?

repetition.boundaries|present|List the limits currently shaping the work, such as its format, available time or materials. Mark which limit helps you make decisions and which has gone unquestioned.|Which constraint gives the project a useful shape, and which is restricting it without a clear purpose?

repetition.boundaries|crossroads|Compare two project directions against one limit you need to protect. Include what you would leave out of each version to keep that limit.|Which option can you pursue without quietly expanding its scope?

repetition.boundaries|action|Write a one-sentence scope for the next work session, including one thing you will leave out. Stop to review when that small scope is complete.|Did the limit help you attend to the work, or does it need adjusting?

repetition.connection|present|Recall one recent exchange about the work. Note what feedback or contribution you asked for, what you received and what remains unclear.|Is outside input helping the project develop, or are you trying to satisfy responses you never asked for?

repetition.connection|crossroads|For two creative directions, list the feedback or collaboration each would need. Separate help already offered from help you are only hoping for.|Which direction has a workable exchange of contributions rather than an assumed audience or partner?

repetition.connection|action|Ask one willing person a precise question about a small part of the draft. Give enough context for that question without asking them to solve the whole project.|What did their response reveal about the work, and what remains your decision?

repetition.solitude|present|Look back at your last period of private work. Identify one observation it produced and one question that has remained unchanged through repeated thought.|Is working alone bringing the piece into focus, or keeping a needed check out of reach?

repetition.solitude|crossroads|Set aside outside reactions briefly and write what interests you in each of two directions. Then mark one private assumption that each option would need to test.|Which preference remains when you are not trying to anticipate an audience?

repetition.solitude|action|Spend ten quiet minutes with one unfinished section. Write down one thing you notice and a specific question to bring into your next review.|What became visible in that pause that you can now use in the work?

repetition.clarity|present|Choose one judgment you have made about the draft. Put the detail you can actually point to beside the interpretation you have given it.|What does the work show, and what are you assuming about how it will be received?

repetition.clarity|crossroads|Name one purpose for the piece and use it to compare the same small section in two possible directions. Apply the same criterion to both.|Which option serves that purpose in a way you can point to, rather than only describe?

repetition.clarity|action|Write one question a small section should answer. Revise only that section, then inspect whether the revision makes its purpose easier to see.|What became clearer, and which claim about the draft still needs checking?

repetition.uncertainty|present|List what is unresolved in one section of the work. Separate an ambiguity you want to keep from a gap that prevents you from developing it.|Which uncertainty is part of the piece, and which is a missing decision or piece of information?

repetition.uncertainty|crossroads|For each of two creative directions, name one unknown that could change your choice. Identify a small check before committing to either.|Which unanswered question matters enough to investigate, and which can remain open?

repetition.uncertainty|action|Make a rough version of one uncertain detail with the materials already available. Record what it helps you learn without treating it as a final answer.|What is now easier to decide, and what did this trial leave unresolved?

repetition.change|present|Compare one current section with what you originally wanted it to do. Mark what still serves that purpose and what no longer does.|Where has the project changed enough that an older approach no longer fits?

repetition.change|crossroads|Sketch two possible revisions of one section, keeping the original beside them. Compare what each preserves and what each asks you to release.|Which revision changes the form while keeping what matters to the work?

repetition.change|action|Save the current version, then revise one small section in a copy. Compare what the change makes clearer before widening it.|What is worth carrying forward from the old version, and what can this revision leave behind?

repetition.stability|present|Identify one routine, tool or stored resource the project relies on. Check whether it still supports the work you are actually making.|What is dependable here, and what are you maintaining mainly because it is familiar?

repetition.stability|crossroads|Compare what two project directions would need to keep going during an ordinary week. Include maintenance and repeated effort, not just the appealing first session.|Which direction has support you can sustain beyond its initial excitement?

repetition.stability|action|Spend ten minutes maintaining one resource the next session needs, such as organized notes, usable materials or a backed-up draft.|What becomes easier to continue once this small support is in place?

repetition.effort|present|Look at the last change you made to the draft. Identify what improved and what received effort without becoming clearer.|Where is practice changing the work, and where are you repeating effort without useful feedback?

repetition.effort|crossroads|Choose two directions and name one skill each would require. Compare the practice and feedback available to you before choosing the more demanding route.|Which challenge can you work on with useful feedback rather than pressure alone?

repetition.effort|action|Practice one difficult detail for ten minutes, keeping the first and last attempts. Compare them before deciding whether more practice is useful today.|What changed through this effort, and what needs a different approach?

repetition.rest|present|Recall how the draft looked before and after your most recent break. Note whether distance changed your judgment or left the same difficulty in place.|Is the work asking for a pause, or for a specific problem to be named once you return?

repetition.rest|crossroads|Compare the pace each of two project directions would require. Include time away from the work and check whether either option depends on constant availability.|Which choice leaves enough distance to keep seeing the work clearly?

repetition.rest|action|Leave one nonessential revision for later and take a short break from the draft. On returning, note one detail before starting to change it.|What can you see after the pause that more polishing was hiding?

repetition.care|present|Name one condition helping the project continue and one that is depleted, such as materials, encouragement or attention. Notice how each affects an actual work session.|What part of the project needs support rather than another demand for output?

repetition.care|crossroads|Compare the attention and materials two directions would need. Include what you need as the maker, not only what a finished piece would require.|Which direction can you tend without treating your own capacity as an unlimited resource?

repetition.care|action|Replenish one small resource before the next session, such as setting out materials or clearing a usable workspace. Keep this preparation smaller than the session it supports.|What support makes returning to the piece more workable without adding another obligation?

repetition.release|present|Choose one element you keep carrying through revisions. Write what it originally contributed and whether that contribution is still needed.|Are you keeping this element for the work it does now, or for the effort already spent on it?

repetition.release|crossroads|Compare two possible directions by naming what each would require you to set aside. Keep a copy of material you are not ready to discard.|Which trade-off can you acknowledge without pretending that leaving something behind is effortless?

repetition.release|action|Move one nonessential element into a separate saved file and try the section without it. Compare the result before deciding whether to keep the change.|What space did removing it create, and what value might still belong elsewhere?

tension.expansion-boundaries|present|Look at one new idea beside the current scope of the project. Name what it could open up and what extra attention or material it would require.|Is this possibility helping the piece develop, or making its limits harder to see?

tension.expansion-boundaries|crossroads|Compare a wider and a narrower version of the project. Give each a trial size and a stopping point before deciding which to pursue.|What could you explore in each version without committing resources you need to protect?

tension.expansion-boundaries|action|Try one new detail in a copy of the draft for ten minutes. Stop to review before allowing it to expand the rest of the project.|Did this opening earn a place in the work within the limit you set?

tension.connection-solitude|present|Look at a section you have kept private. Identify what is becoming clearer on your own and one question an outside response could help you examine.|What needs room to develop privately, and what is staying unclear because it has not been checked?

tension.connection-solitude|crossroads|For each of two directions, decide what you need to work out privately and what feedback you would want before committing. Check whether that feedback is available.|Which choice gives you room to form a view while leaving it open to a useful response?

tension.connection-solitude|action|Work privately on one small section, then write a precise feedback question for a willing reader or collaborator. Ask it when a suitable person is available.|What are you ready to share for feedback without handing over the whole creative decision?

tension.change-stability|present|Name one part of the project that still works and one that no longer fits. Look at a concrete example of each before treating the whole piece as a problem.|What can remain dependable while you reconsider the part that needs revision?

tension.change-stability|crossroads|Compare two revisions while keeping one useful element constant. Note what each change improves and what support it would disrupt.|Which change addresses the actual problem while preserving something the work still needs?

tension.change-stability|action|Save the draft and change one small section while leaving its strongest supporting element intact. Review the result before altering anything else.|What improved because it changed, and what helped because it stayed steady?

tension.effort-rest|present|Look at a recent stretch of work and mark where useful changes gave way to repeated adjustments. Include what happened to your attention at that point.|Where does continued effort stop teaching you anything about the piece?

tension.effort-rest|crossroads|Compare the work sessions two directions would need, including breaks and review. Notice if either route assumes you can keep pushing without losing perspective.|Which direction has a pace that supports both making and seeing what you have made?

tension.effort-rest|action|Choose one detail for a ten-minute work session, then step away before judging it. Compare it with the earlier version after the pause.|Did the work, the pause or their combination make the next decision clearer?

tension.clarity-uncertainty|present|Look at one unfinished section. Separate what the draft already shows from what you are still guessing about its effect.|Which uncertainty belongs to the work itself, and which comes from not having shown or tested it yet?

tension.clarity-uncertainty|crossroads|Name two directions for the piece. For each, write what you know from the draft and one unanswered question that could change your choice.|What would you need to see or hear before preferring one direction?

tension.clarity-uncertainty|action|Make a rough alternate version of one small section to test a single unanswered question. Compare it with the original before polishing either.|What did that comparison clarify, and what can remain undecided?

tension.care-boundaries|present|Name what is sustaining the project and what maintaining it is costing you. Mark one demand that is taking attention from the work you want to support.|Which part of caring for this work has become pressure to keep every part alive?

tension.care-boundaries|crossroads|For each project direction, compare the attention it needs with the time and materials you can provide. Name one limit you will protect in either choice.|Which direction leaves enough capacity to tend the work without treating exhaustion as proof of commitment?

tension.care-boundaries|action|Reduce one nonessential demand on the next session so you can support a neglected part of the project within your present capacity. Stop at a limit chosen beforehand.|What support helped the work, and what demand could stay outside the next session?

complement.clarity-effort|present|Choose one recent task and name the creative question it was meant to answer. Compare that purpose with the change it actually produced.|Is the effort following a clear question, or has doing more replaced deciding what the work needs?

complement.clarity-effort|crossroads|For each of two directions, state one creative aim and the smallest task that could test it. Compare what the results would let you learn before choosing.|Which route connects a purpose you can explain with an attempt you can realistically make?

complement.clarity-effort|action|Write one question about a small part of the draft, then give yourself ten minutes to test it with a revision. Keep the earlier version for comparison.|What did the attempt reveal about the question, rather than about your worth as a maker?

complement.care-connection|present|Identify one need affecting the project, then look at how you have communicated it to anyone involved. Separate a request you have made from a response you have merely hoped for.|What would another person need to understand before their contribution could actually help?

complement.care-connection|crossroads|Compare the support each creative direction would need. For one consequential contribution, check whether someone is willing and able to offer it before building the choice around it.|Which support is genuinely available, and which option depends on an unspoken expectation?

complement.care-connection|action|Name one manageable contribution that would help the work and ask a suitable person whether they are willing to provide it. Leave room to adjust the plan if they decline.|How did stating the need change your understanding of what support is possible?

complement.release-change|present|Find one part of the draft whose purpose has ended. Note whether continuing to maintain it is blocking a revision you already want to examine.|What change has less room to develop because you are still carrying an exhausted element?

complement.release-change|crossroads|For each of two revisions, name what you would set aside and what that would make possible. Save the original so the comparison does not require an irreversible deletion.|Which revision creates useful space instead of simply adding another layer of work?

complement.release-change|action|Save a copy, remove one element that no longer serves the piece, then try one small revision in the space it leaves.|What could the work do after that release that it could not do while everything stayed in place?
